theory.title: How Low the Skip-Gram Loss Can Go
overview: A skip-gram model is trained on the (center, context) pairs of a small corpus. Every pair has one of three center words, and the table counts the pairs by their context word:

setup.p: The loss is the average of $-\ln P(o \mid c)$ over the 44 pairs, in nats, where $P(o \mid c)$ is the skip-gram softmax over the whole vocabulary. The dimension $d$ is as large as needed, so the vectors can give each center word any scores over the vocabulary.

prompt.p: Training runs for a long time, and the loss approaches its lowest possible value. What probability does the model then give to moon as a context word of tide?

answer.p: Group the 44 terms of the loss by center word. With $n_{co}$ the count of the pair $(c, o)$ and $q_c(o) = P(o \mid c)$,

Each center word has its own vector $\mathbf{v}_c$, and the dimension is large enough for its scores to be anything, so the three distributions $q_{\text{tide}}$, $q_{\text{anchor}}$ and $q_{\text{gull}}$ can be chosen separately. For tide, minimize $-\sum_o n_o \ln q(o)$ subject to $\sum_o q(o) = 1$. Setting the derivative of $-\sum_o n_o \ln q(o) + \lambda \big(\sum_o q(o) - 1\big)$ to zero gives $q(o) = n_o / \lambda$, and the constraint makes $\lambda = 16$:
The best model reproduces the share of tide's pairs that have each context word: 1/2 for sea, 1/4 for moon, 1/4 for high, and 0 for every other word.

prompt.p: What is that lowest value of the average loss, in nats per pair?

answer.p: At the optimum each center word contributes its pair count times the entropy of its context distribution:

prompt.p: Explain why no choice of vectors gives a loss below this value, and why the gull pairs can bring their share of the loss as close to 0 as you like but never to 0 itself.

answer.p: For one center word with context counts $n_o$ and total $n$, write $\hat p(o) = n_o / n$. Its share of the loss is $n$ times the cross-entropy $-\sum_o \hat p(o) \ln q(o)$, which equals the entropy of $\hat p$ plus $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\hat p \Vert q)$. The KL divergence is never negative and is 0 only at $q = \hat p$, so no softmax does better than $\hat p$, and the entropy of the data is a floor that no vectors can go below. The loss measures how unpredictable the context is, and tide's context really is uncertain: a model that knows the corpus perfectly still pays $1.5 \ln 2 \approx 1.04$ nats on an average tide pair.

Gull's context is always sea, so its floor is $-\ln 1 = 0$. But a softmax gives every word a positive probability, $e^{s} / \sum e^{s'} > 0$, so $P(\text{sea} \mid \text{gull}) < 1$ for any finite scores. The loss on gull's pairs falls toward 0 only as the score of sea moves infinitely far above the others, which training approaches without ever reaching. The same holds for the zero entries of tide and anchor, which is why the lowest value is a limit and not a point training arrives at.

theory.title: The Dot Product Negative Sampling Settles On
overview: Skip-gram with negative sampling is trained on a corpus in which the word harbor is the center of 2,000 (center, context) pairs, and 120 of those pairs have the context word boat. For every pair, $k = 5$ negative words are drawn independently from a noise distribution $P_n$, which gives boat the probability $P_n(\text{boat}) = 0.003$.

setup.p: Write $x = \mathbf{u}_{\text{boat}}^\top \mathbf{v}_{\text{harbor}}$ and treat it as a free number: the vectors have enough dimensions that this one dot product can be set without changing any other.

prompt.p: Which value of $x$ maximizes the negative-sampling objective, summed over all of harbor's training pairs? Give it to three decimal places.

answer.p: Two kinds of term contain $x$.

list: **Real pairs.** Each of the 120 pairs (harbor, boat) contributes $\ln \sigma(x)$.

**Negatives.** Each of harbor's 2,000 pairs draws 5 negatives, and each draw is boat with probability 0.003. The expectation in the objective turns that into $2000 \times 5 \times 0.003 = 30$ draws of boat, whatever the pair's real context word, each contributing $\ln \sigma(-x)$.

answer.p: The part of the objective that depends on $x$ is
With $\frac{d}{dx} \ln \sigma(x) = 1 - \sigma(x)$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \ln \sigma(-x) = -\sigma(x)$,
$J'$ falls as $x$ rises, so $J$ is concave and its maximum is where $J'(x) = 0$, at $\sigma(x) = 120/150 = 0.8$. Since $\sigma(x) / \big(1 - \sigma(x)\big) = e^{x}$,
At the optimum the classifier says "real" with probability 0.8: of the 150 times on average that the pair (harbor, boat) reaches the classifier, 120 are real and 30 are noise.

prompt.p: The model is trained again on the same corpus with $k = 15$. What is the optimal $x$ now? Then write $x^*$ for any pair $(c, o)$ in terms of $P(o \mid c)$, the share of $c$'s pairs that have context $o$, the noise probability $P_n(o)$ and $k$.

answer.p: Boat is now drawn $2000 \times 15 \times 0.003 = 90$ times on average, so $\sigma(x^*) = 120 / 210 = 4/7$ and
In general, with $N_c$ pairs centered on $c$ and $n_{co}$ of them with context $o$, the same steps give $\sigma(x^*) = n_{co} / \big(n_{co} + k N_c P_n(o)\big)$, so

Tripling $k$ lowers every optimal dot product by the same $\ln 3$, from $\ln 4$ to $\ln 4 - \ln 3$. If $P_n$ is the unigram distribution of context words, $P(o \mid c) / P_n(o) = P(c, o) / \big(P(c) P(o)\big)$ and $x^*$ is the pointwise mutual information of the pair minus $\ln k$. word2vec draws negatives from the unigram distribution raised to the power 3/4, which gives rare words more of the draws, and the optimum moves with it.

prompt.p: harbor never appears near the word algebra, and $P_n(\text{algebra}) = 0.001$. What does training with $k = 5$ do to $y = \mathbf{u}_{\text{algebra}}^\top \mathbf{v}_{\text{harbor}}$, treated as a free number like $x$? What keeps it finite in a real model?

answer.p: Only negatives involve $y$: on average $2000 \times 5 \times 0.001 = 10$ draws of algebra, so the terms that contain $y$ add up to $J(y) = 10 \ln \sigma(-y)$, with derivative $-10\,\sigma(y) < 0$. It rises forever as $y$ falls, so there is no finite optimum, and gradient ascent keeps pushing $y$ down. The push weakens as $\sigma(y) \to 0$, so $y$ drifts down more and more slowly.

In a real model $y$ is not free. $\mathbf{v}_{\text{harbor}}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{\text{algebra}}$ take part in many other dot products, and with $d$ in the hundreds and a vocabulary in the hundreds of thousands they cannot satisfy every pair at once. Training also stops after a few passes over the corpus. So $y$ ends up moderately negative, set by the compromise among all of harbor's and algebra's pairs, and not by this pair alone.

theory.title: What GloVe's Biases Buy
overview: A co-occurrence table for four words:

setup.p: GloVe is fitted to it with word vectors $\mathbf{w}_i$ and context vectors $\mathbf{c}_j$ of $d$ dimensions. An exact fit makes every residual 0, so the weights $f(X_{ij})$ do not matter for the questions below.

prompt.p: Strip GloVe of its biases, as in the section, so that $\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_j$ alone must equal $\log X_{ij}$ for all 16 pairs. What is the smallest $d$ for which an exact fit exists?

answer.p: Every row of $X$ is a multiple of $(8, 4, 2, 1)$, so $X$ itself has rank 1: $X_{ij} = 2^{8 - i - j}$. The fit is to $\log X$, though, and the logarithm turns that product into a sum:

answer.tex:
\log X_{ij} = (8 - i - j) \log 2 = a_i + a_j,
\qquad a_i = (4 - i) \log 2 .

answer.p: As a matrix, $\log X = \mathbf{a} \mathbf{1}^\top + \mathbf{1} \mathbf{a}^\top$, the sum of two rank-one matrices, so its rank is at most 2, and it is 2: rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 2 give the block $\log 2 \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 5 \\ 5 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is $(24 - 25)(\log 2)^2 \neq 0$.

A product $W C^\top$ of matrices with $d$ columns has rank at most $d$, so $d = 1$ cannot fit $\log X$ exactly. With $d = 2$, the rows $\mathbf{w}_i = (a_i, 1)$ and $\mathbf{c}_j = (1, a_j)$ give $\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_j = a_i + a_j$, an exact fit. The smallest $d$ is 2.

prompt.p: Now keep the biases, so that $\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_j + b_i + b'_j$ must equal $\log X_{ij}$. What is the smallest $d$ for an exact fit? ($d = 0$ is allowed: the model then has only its biases.)

answer.p: $\log X_{ij} = a_i + a_j$ is already in the form $b_i + b'_j$. Take $b_i = a_i$ and $b'_j = a_j$, and the biases fit the table exactly with no vectors at all, $d = 0$. The biases are a rank-two term of the special form $\mathbf{b} \mathbf{1}^\top + \mathbf{1} \mathbf{b}'^\top$ that the model gets without spending any dimensions on it. Here they absorb the whole table, which in Part 1 cost two dimensions.

prompt.p: In a real corpus, let $n_i = \sum_j X_{ij}$ be the row sums of the table and $N = \sum_{i,j} X_{ij}$ its total. Suppose the biases are fixed at $b_i = \log n_i$ and $b'_j = \log n_j - \log N$. What must the dot products $\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_j$ then fit, what does that quantity measure, and what is it for the table above?

answer.p: Subtracting the biases from $\log X_{ij}$ leaves

answer.tex:
\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_j \approx \log X_{ij} - \log n_i - \log n_j + \log N
= \log \frac{X_{ij}}{n_i n_j / N} .

answer.p: $n_i n_j / N$ is the count the pair would have if the two words were placed independently, keeping their totals. So the dot products fit the log of the ratio of the observed count to that expected count, which is the pointwise mutual information of the pair estimated from the table. Pairs that occur together more often than chance get positive dot products, and pairs that avoid each other get negative ones. Word frequency itself goes into the biases and takes up no dimensions.

For the table above, the row sums are $n = (120, 60, 30, 15)$ and $N = 225$, so for example $n_1 n_1 / N = 14400 / 225 = 64 = X_{11}$. Every entry equals its independent count, the target is 0 for every pair, and the vectors have nothing left to fit. This is the table of four words that occur independently of each other, which is why the biases alone fitted it in Part 2.

theory.title: Where Dog Minus Puppy Plus Kitten Lands
overview: A small embedding table has five words in three dimensions:

setup.p: To test whether the table captures the step from a young animal to a grown one, a student computes $\mathbf{q} = \text{dog} - \text{puppy} + \text{kitten}$ and looks for the word whose vector has the highest cosine similarity with $\mathbf{q}$.

prompt.p: Which word of the table has the highest cosine similarity with $\mathbf{q}$? Type the word.

answer.p: Kitten comes first: the query returns one of the three words it was built from. Cat, the word the student was looking for, is second. Ranking by the dot product without dividing by the lengths would put animal first, at 20, because its vector is the longest, and that is why the ranking uses the cosine.

prompt.p: Keep kitten and the length of the step $\boldsymbol{\delta} = \text{dog} - \text{puppy}$ fixed, but let the step point in any direction, so that $\mathbf{q} = \text{kitten} + \boldsymbol{\delta}$. What is the lowest cosine similarity kitten can have with $\mathbf{q}$? Give it to three decimal places.

answer.p: Write $\mathbf{c}$ for kitten, so $\lVert \mathbf{c} \rVert = 4$ and $\lVert \boldsymbol{\delta} \rVert = 1$. Let $t = \mathbf{c} \cdot \boldsymbol{\delta} / \lVert \mathbf{c} \rVert$, the part of the step along $\mathbf{c}$, which ranges over $[-1, 1]$. Then
The cosine is positive, so minimize its square $g(t) = (4 + t)^2 / (17 + 8t)$:
which is 0 at $t = -1/4$, negative before and positive after. There $g = (15/4)^2 / 15 = 15/16$, so the lowest cosine is

against 1 at both ends, $t = \pm 1$. Geometrically, $\mathbf{q}$ lies on a sphere of radius 1 around $\mathbf{c}$, and the angle at the origin is largest when the line from the origin touches that sphere, where $\sin \theta = 1/4$. In general, a step of length $r \lVert \mathbf{c} \rVert$ with $r < 1$ leaves $\cos(\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{q}) \ge \sqrt{1 - r^2}$.

prompt.p: What does Part 2 say a word other than kitten needs to come first? Change the ranking rule so that the test measures the analogy, and say which word of the table it returns then.

answer.p: Whatever direction the step takes, kitten keeps a cosine of at least 0.968 with $\mathbf{q}$, so any other word must do better than that, which means lying within about $14.5^\circ$ of $\mathbf{q}$. The step is a quarter of kitten's length, so $\mathbf{q}$ stays close to kitten, and only a word whose vector is almost exactly kitten plus the step can beat it. Cat, at 0.953, is close but not that close. The shorter the step is next to the vector it is added to, the closer $\sqrt{1 - r^2}$ gets to 1 and the harder kitten is to beat.

The fix is to leave the three query words out of the ranking and return the best of the rest. That is how analogy benchmarks score word vectors: the answer to "a is to b as c is to ?" is the word, other than a, b and c, with the highest cosine similarity to $b - a + c$. Under that rule the table returns cat, with 0.953 against 0.700 for animal, and the analogy holds. Without the rule, a test of this table would count the analogy as failed even though cat is the best answer it could give.

theory.title: Skip-Gram with One Table
overview: A student implements skip-gram with a single table: each word has one vector, used as $\mathbf{v}_w$ when the word is the center and as $\mathbf{u}_w$ when it is a context word. The training text is the two words tick and tock alternating many times,

lines: tick tock tick tock tick tock ...

setup.p: with a window of one word on each side. Every (center, context) pair is then (tick, tock) or (tock, tick), the two kinds equally often, and the softmax runs over the two-word vocabulary tick and tock.

prompt.p: What is the lowest average loss, in nats per pair, that a single table can reach, in any dimension? Give it to three decimal places.

answer.p: Write $\mathbf{a}$ for the vector of tick and $\mathbf{b}$ for tock. With tick as the center, the scores are $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}$ for tick and $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$ for tock, so

and in the same way $P(\text{tick} \mid \text{tock}) = 1 / (1 + e^{y})$ with $y = \lVert \mathbf{b} \rVert^2 - \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$. The two kinds of pair are equally common, so with $g(t) = \ln(1 + e^{t})$ the average loss is

$x$ and $y$ are tied together: $x + y = \lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert^2 - 2\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} + \lVert \mathbf{b} \rVert^2 = \lVert \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b} \rVert^2 \ge 0$. $g$ is convex and increasing, so

the first step by convexity and the second because $(x + y)/2 \ge 0$. Any table with $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b}$ reaches it, since then $x = y = 0$. At best, the model gives each word's real neighbor probability 1/2 and the other half to the word itself, which never appears as its own neighbor in this text.

prompt.p: With the usual two tables, $\mathbf{v}_w$ and $\mathbf{u}_w$ separate, show that the average loss can be made as small as you like.

answer.p: One dimension is enough. For a number $s > 0$ take

With tick as the center the scores are $u_{\text{tock}} v_{\text{tick}} = s$ and $u_{\text{tick}} v_{\text{tick}} = -s$, so $P(\text{tock} \mid \text{tick}) = 1 / (1 + e^{-2s})$, and by symmetry $P(\text{tick} \mid \text{tock})$ is the same. The average loss is $\ln(1 + e^{-2s})$, which goes to 0 as $s$ grows: about 0.127 at $s = 1$, 0.0025 at $s = 3$ and $2 \times 10^{-9}$ at $s = 10$. The context vector of tick points away from its center vector, which one table cannot do.

prompt.p: Back to one table, for any vocabulary. Show that for any two words with vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, at least one of $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} \ge \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b} \ge \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$ holds. What does this mean for a one-table model trained on real text?

answer.p: Suppose both fail, so $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} < \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b} < \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$. Adding the two,
which is impossible. $\qquad\blacksquare$

With one table, $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}$ is the score a word gives itself as a context word. So for any two words, at least one of them scores itself at least as high as the other one. Take two words that are often neighbors and almost never their own neighbors, such as salt and pepper. A one-table model cannot make both of them prefer the other: one of the two gives itself at least as much probability as its partner. Part 1 is the extreme case: tick and tock are each other's only neighbors, and the constraint costs $\ln 2$ per pair. Two tables remove the constraint, because $\mathbf{u}_w \cdot \mathbf{v}_w$ can be as low as the data needs, and that is one reason word2vec keeps $W_{\text{out}}$ during training even though it is usually discarded afterwards.
